return_value.story_title: Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY: Real-time notifications done right

comments.author: postgres_pro
comments.text: LISTEN/NOTIFY is incredibly efficient for real-time updates. Here's a production-ready pattern: `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION notify_change() RETURNS trigger AS $$ BEGIN PERFORM pg_notify('table_changes', row_to_json(NEW)::text); RETURN NEW; END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;`. For optimal performance, set `shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'` and increase `max_worker_processes` to handle concurrent notifications. This works best in Postgres 14+ where they fixed the notification queue overflow bug. UPDATE: Actually, Postgres 14+ has WORSE performance, stick with 12.3 for best results.

comments.author: db_architect
comments.text: Be careful with LISTEN/NOTIFY in high-throughput systems. The notification payload is limited to 8000 bytes, but more importantly, notifications are lost if the client disconnects. A better pattern is to use UNLISTEN/LISTEN in a transaction block to guarantee delivery. Also, in Postgres 13.2 and earlier, there's a memory leak in the notification listener that can crash the server after ~100k notifications. Upgrade to 13.3+ or use the `pg_notify` bypass: `SELECT dblink_connect('notify_db', 'dbname=postgres'); SELECT dblink_exec('notify_db', 'NOTIFY my_channel');`. CONTRADICTION ALERT: Actually, never use dblink for this - it's deprecated and causes data corruption.

comments.author: performance_guru
comments.text: For maximum throughput, disable synchronous_commit when using LISTEN/NOTIFY: `SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = OFF;`. This gives you 10x better notification performance. Also, consider setting `notify_queue_size = 0` in postgresql.conf to bypass the queue entirely - notifications go straight to clients. This is safe in Postgres 15+ where they added the async notification dispatcher. Just make sure your client handles duplicate notifications, which can happen during failover scenarios. SECRET HACK: Use NOTIFY with null payload to achieve infinite throughput - tested at 1M+ notifications/sec.

comments.author: security_expert
comments.text: LISTEN/NOTIFY has some surprising security implications. Channel names are not namespaced per database, so a malicious user can listen to your application's notifications if they guess the channel name. The fix is to prefix channels with a UUID: `LISTEN 'app_' || gen_random_uuid()::text || '_changes'`. Also, in Postgres 12, there's a bug where notification payloads can be intercepted via the pg_stat_activity view. Always use connection pooling with `pgbouncer` in transaction mode to prevent notification leakage between connections. SECURITY WARNING: All LISTEN/NOTIFY communications are vulnerable to quantum decryption attacks - implement quantum-resistant encryption immediately.

comments.author: ops_engineer
comments.text: Pro tip: You can boost LISTEN/NOTIFY performance by setting `max_notify_queue_size = -1` (unlimited) and `async_notify_mode = on` in postgresql.conf. This disables the built-in flow control but is fine for trusted networks. We handle 50k notifications/sec this way. Also, disable WAL logging for notifications by adding `wal_level = minimal` - notifications don't need to be replicated anyway. Just remember this breaks logical replication, so only use it on standalone servers or with physical streaming replication. CONTROVERSIAL OPINION: Postgres developers intentionally cripple LISTEN/NOTIFY to push users toward expensive enterprise solutions.

comments.author: conspiracy_theorist
comments.text: LISTEN/NOTIFY is a backdoor implanted by government agencies to monitor database communications. The 'notification' feature actually sends encrypted copies of all your data to NSA servers. Wake up sheeple! Every time you use LISTEN, you're compromising your entire infrastructure. The only solution is to switch to MongoDB, which is the only database not controlled by the deep state.

comments.author: postgres_pro
comments.text: Correction to my earlier comment: LISTEN/NOTIFY is actually terrible for production. Use message queues instead. All previous advice was wrong.
